citation.title: Equivariant neural operators for gradient-consistent topology optimization
citation.venue: Journal of Computational Design and Engineering 11(3) (2024) 91-100 (Oxford University Press; advance access 19 April 2024; open access, CC BY 4.0)
citation.version_coded: Version of record: the typeset journal PDF (10 pp.) deposited in Apollo, the University of Cambridge repository (hdl 1810/367947; OpenAlex labels this copy submittedVersion), read in full as text. Page locators are journal pages 91-100

included.reason: I-SPEED (screening code confirmed at full text; the article's stated focus and its only ML-vs-classical time comparison is SIMP run time with learned vs finite-difference PDE solvers, Table 2)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: On SELTO disc test problems (39×39×4 voxels), SIMP with a learned neural-operator PDE solver runs in 2-19 s versus 75 s with the classical finite-difference solver on the same Xeon Silver 4210 CPU, stated as at least fourfold faster.
claim.key_phrase: all NO models provide at least a fourfold improvement in inference speed
claim.location: Sec. 5.3, p. 96, and Table 2, p. 97 (main text; the abstract, introduction and conclusion hold no quantitative classical comparison). Chosen under §5.1 rule 4 over the earlier Table 1 (IoU against the SIMP designs, p. 96), because the article states its focus is a speed-up of classical SIMP (p. 96)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Stated as at least fourfold (p. 96). Table 2 averages: FDM SIMP 75 s; learned solvers 2-3 s without equivariance and 15-19 s with equivariance, i.e. 25-37.5× and 3.9-5× [derived]. The best-quality model (equivariant U-Net FNO, 19 s) gives 3.9× [derived], just below the stated floor. One FDM solve at 160,000 voxels takes almost 5 min vs under 1 s for a NO (p. 96; on the order of 300× per solve [derived]). Training (2-14 h) and data generation are excluded.
claim.alternatives: (1) Table 1 (p. 96), quality against the SIMP ground truth: best IoU 0.73 with fail% 6.25 and mean compliance 0.56 (equivariant U-Net FNO, 200 trajectories); across models and data sizes IoU 0.29-0.73 and fail% 6.25-73.75; the SIMP reference's own fail% and compliance are not given (stratum Q if chosen). (2) p. 96: one FDM solve at 160,000 voxels takes almost 5 min vs under 1 s for a NO. (3) Abstract, background: NOs offer large speed-ups over classical PDE solvers (not this article's measurement).

baseline.classical_method: SIMP compliance minimization with a finite-difference (FDM) linear-elasticity solver, 60 iterations per problem; the learned operator replaces only the PDE solve inside the same SIMP loop (Sec. 4-5)
baseline.implementation: DL4TO, the authors' PyTorch library (Sec. 5.1); public on GitHub under Apache-2.0 per the GitHub API (2026-09-24); the FDM solver's linear algebra is not described in the article
baseline.solver: not stated (finite-difference discretization; linear solver not stated)
baseline.hardware_ml: the same Intel Xeon Silver 4210 CPU for the timed runs (Table 2); training on a GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU (Sec. 5.1)
baseline.problem_size: 39×39×4 voxel grid of the SELTO disc dataset (Sec. 5.1) [derived: about 2.4×10^4 DOFs, 40×40×5 nodes × 3]; one finer example with 160,000 voxels (p. 96)
baseline.classical_iterations: 60 SIMP iterations per problem (i_max = 60, Sec. 5.1); the timed runs are assumed to use the same count [inferred]
baseline.classical_time: 75 s average per SIMP run (Table 2) [derived: about 1.25 s per iteration]; almost 5 min for one FDM solve at 160,000 voxels (p. 96)
baseline.ml_time: Average per SIMP run with the learned solver: U-Net 2 s, FNO 3 s, U-FNO 3 s, U-Net FNO 3 s without equivariance; 15, 18, 17 and 19 s with equivariance (Table 2)
baseline.training_time: 2-14 h per model on an RTX 2080 Ti, 100-1000 epochs (Sec. 5.1, p. 95)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; 10-200 SIMP trajectories of 60 iterations from the SELTO disc dataset, i.e. 600-12,000 samples (Sec. 5.1) [inferred: about 4.2 h for 200 trajectories at the 75 s Table 2 average]
baseline.quality_metric: IoU with the SIMP ground-truth design, fail% (von Mises stress above 1.1× the yield stress, or a loaded voxel not connected to the supports) and mean compliance of the final designs (Table 1); WMAE of the density trajectory (Fig. 6)
baseline.quality_gap: Best: IoU 0.73, fail% 6.25, compliance 0.56 (equivariant U-Net FNO, 200 trajectories); range IoU 0.29-0.73, fail% 6.25-73.75, compliance 0.56-4.52 (Table 1). The SIMP reference's own fail% and compliance are not reported

R1.evidence: Tables 1-2 and Sec. 5.3: both runs use the same 60-iteration SIMP loop [inferred], and quality is reported, but the learned-solver designs match the SIMP designs only in part (best IoU 0.73) and 6.25-73.75% of them fail the stress or connectivity check, while the SIMP reference's fail% and compliance are not given. No matching is attempted; the authors acknowledge a quality-speed trade-off (p. 96). If these numbers are read as measurably worse than SIMP, R1-unmatched (fail) applies.

R2.evidence: Table 2 and p. 96: the FDM SIMP takes 75 s for 60 iterations at about 2.4×10^4 DOFs, about 1.25 s per iteration [derived], one FDM solve at 160,000 voxels takes almost 5 min, and the authors state that FDM cost grows quadratically with the voxel count. This looks slow for the size [inferred], but the linear solver is not stated and no direct comparison is possible. Both methods run on the same CPU, so (c) does not apply; (b) not observed; (d) not established (no convergence criterion or plot). Pointer for (e): 1.25 s per iteration at 39×39×4 [derived].

R3.evidence: Sec. 5.1 and 5.3: training time is reported (2-14 h) and the data need is discussed only qualitatively; the data-generation cost is not reported and no break-even is given. For C3 [derived]: 200 trajectories at the 75 s average (15,000 s) plus 7,200-50,400 s of training, against a saving of 56 s per run for the equivariant U-Net FNO (75 − 19), break even after about 400-1,170 runs; for the fastest model (73 s saved), after about 300-900 runs.

R4.evidence: Sec. 5.2 and Table 1: the final design of every test problem is scored by IoU, compliance and a failure check (stress above 1.1× yield, or loaded voxels disconnected from the supports), and failures are counted (fail%). The article does not say which solver scores the designs [classical solver inferred]; volume fractions are not reported. Unsure, so pass.

reporting.n_test_cases: The SELTO disc test split (size not stated) for each of 32 model settings: 4 architectures × with/without equivariance × 4 training-set sizes (Table 1)

notes: Primary-outcome judgment: no quantitative classical comparison appears in the abstract, introduction or conclusion (the abstract's speed statement is background on neural operators in general). In the main text, Table 1 (IoU against the SIMP ground truth) precedes the timing, but its comparisons are mainly among neural-operator architectures, and the article states its focus is a speed-up of classical SIMP (p. 96), so the Table 2 speed comparison is taken under §5.1 rule 4; Table 1 is the quality alternative. The stated floor of fourfold does not hold for the equivariant U-Net FNO, the configuration with the best quality (75/19 = 3.9 [derived]). The 160,000-voxel timing (p. 96) gives no mesh, solver or hardware details. runtimes_all_cases = yes: Table 2 gives averages per solver, taken to cover the test set [inferred]. Access: the OUP PDF link listed by OpenAlex answered curl with HTTP 403 (not pursued); the Apollo copy is the typeset version of record (journal header, CC BY). Code: no code link for the neural operators; the SIMP side runs in the public DL4TO library (Apache-2.0), and the SELTO dataset is on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.7034898), so a baseline-only re-test at 39×39×4 is possible. retest_candidate false because the neural-operator models are not public. Duplicate check: no other version in the pool; P00114 (SELTO), P00817 (DL4TO) and P01614 (SELTO dataset) by the same group are different works. No author named Jun Wang. Screening code was I-SPEED.
